title: Remove Covered Intervals
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every pair versus sorting by start (end descending for ties) and tracking a running maximum end in one pass.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of intervals, remove all intervals that are covered by another interval in the list. Interval [a,b] is covered by [c,d] if c <= a and b <= d. Return the number of remaining intervals after removing all covered ones.

blocks.text: An interval is covered if some other interval starts no later and ends no earlier. Sorting by start ascending, with ties broken by end DESCENDING, ensures that whenever two intervals share a start, the longer one (which would cover the shorter one) is processed first, letting a running "maximum end seen so far" directly detect coverage.

blocks.title: Analogy: Removing Redundant Overlapping Warranty Periods
blocks.text: Picture several warranty periods for the same item, some of which are entirely subsumed by longer ones covering the exact same or a wider range. Sorting by start date, and for same-start warranties keeping the longer one processed first, lets a single pass identify and discard every warranty that adds no new coverage beyond what has already been seen.

blocks.caption: Sorting by start ascending (end descending for ties) lets a running max-end track coverage in one pass

Before checking every pair of intervals for containment, notice that sorting by start ascending (with a specific tie-break) lets a single running "maximum end" value directly reveal whether each subsequent interval is covered, since anything covered must end no later than something already fully processed.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If interval B's start is greater than or equal to interval A's start, and B's end is less than or equal to A's end, B is covered by A.

Observation 2: Sorting by start ascending groups intervals with the SAME or later start together in a way that a running "maximum end seen so far" (from a previous interval with an equal or smaller start) directly reveals coverage: if the current interval's end is <= this running max, it is covered.

Observation 3: For intervals sharing the exact same start, breaking ties by end DESCENDING ensures the LONGER (covering) one is processed first, so the shorter one correctly registers as covered by it.

Observation 4: Counting only the intervals whose end STRICTLY EXCEEDS the running maximum end (updating that maximum whenever it does) gives exactly the count of intervals that are NOT covered by anything processed so far.

This leads to sorting by start ascending (end descending for ties), then a single pass counting an interval only if its end exceeds the running maximum end seen so far, updating that maximum as it goes.
Check every pair of intervals directly, marking one as covered if another interval's range fully contains it.

items: For each interval i, check every other interval j.
If interval j covers interval i (j starts no later and ends no earlier), mark i as covered.
Count the intervals that are never marked as covered by any other.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Checking every pair directly implements the coverage definition, correct regardless of order.
This costs O(n squared), unnecessary once sorting lets a single pass detect coverage in O(n log n) total.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared).
Space: O(n) for the covered tracking array.
Limitation: sorting first (with the right tie-break) lets a single running maximum reveal coverage directly, achieving O(n log n) instead of O(n squared).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every pair is unnecessary: once sorted by start (with the right tie-break), coverage of an interval by an EARLIER-processed one is fully captured by whether its end exceeds the running maximum end seen so far.

The critical tie-break: sorting ties (same start) by end DESCENDING ensures the covering (longer) interval is processed before the covered (shorter) one, since both share the exact same start value.

The single-pass counting rule: an interval counts as "not covered" only if its end strictly exceeds the running maximum end; if so, update that maximum; otherwise, it is covered by something already processed.

The core idea: sort once with a careful tie-break, then a single O(n) pass using a running maximum end to detect and skip covered intervals.
Sort intervals by start ascending, end descending for ties. In a single pass, count an interval only if its end exceeds the running maximum end seen so far, updating that maximum whenever it does.

blocks.caption: A single pass with a running maximum end correctly detects and skips covered intervals

codes.python:
def remove_covered_intervals(intervals):
    intervals.sort(key=lambda x: (x[0], -x[1]))          # start asc, end desc for ties
    count = 0
    prev_end = float('-inf')
    for start, end in intervals:
        if end > prev_end:                                  # not covered by anything so far
            count += 1
            prev_end = end
    return count

blocks.text: Sorting by start ascending guarantees every interval processed later starts no earlier than the running maximum end's originating interval, so if its end does not exceed that running maximum, it must be fully covered by that earlier interval (or one contributing to that maximum). The end-descending tie-break specifically handles same-start intervals correctly, ensuring the longer one is registered first so the shorter, same-start interval is correctly recognized as covered.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by the sort.
Space: O(1) extra (or O(n) if the sort is not in-place).

blocks.text: Remove Covered Intervals demonstrates how a carefully chosen sort tie-break (end descending, not just start ascending) is what enables a simple single-pass running-maximum technique to correctly detect coverage.

items: Forgetting the end-descending tie-break for equal starts, which would incorrectly treat the shorter interval as processed before (and thus not covered by) the longer one.
Using "<" instead of "<=" (or vice versa) in the coverage check, mishandling exact boundary matches.

blocks.text: If the interviewer says "remove intervals fully contained in another", think: sort by start ascending, end descending for ties, then track a running maximum end in one pass.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Checking every pair costs O(n squared) time; sorting with the correct tie-break plus a single pass costs O(n log n) time, both using minimal extra space.

items: Pattern: sort by start ascending (end descending for ties), then a single pass using a running maximum end to detect coverage.
Core Idea: count an interval only if its end exceeds the running maximum end seen so far, updating that maximum as the pass proceeds.
Time: O(n squared) for checking every pair, O(n log n) for the sort-plus-single-pass approach.
Most Important Observation: the end-descending tie-break for equal starts is essential for correctly detecting coverage among same-start intervals.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known interval problem rewarding careful attention to sort tie-breaking.
One line memory trick: sort start asc, end desc; count only if end beats the running max.
